An open-window test is a useful migration baseline: sign in, open a screen, check its initial state, close it, verify cleanup, and sign out.

SIMULATED C# WALKTHROUGH · ACTIVE STEP HIGHLIGHTED

Execution observations

    Retry timeout: 1.8 seconds, polling every 100ms. A failure stops the walkthrough; teardown closes the mock window and signs out. Stop & reset cancels pending rendering and observations. This demonstrates the proposed helper behavior, not a verified implementation of the original framework.

    The contract stays recognizable.

    The supplied example checks titles, four visible tabs, one enabled tab, the default selection, focused and required fields, empty values, unchecked flags, and browser-page cleanup. The async rewrite also adds a heading assertion.

    The goal is traceable coverage. Similar-looking code alone does not prove that selectors, timing, or close behavior work in the new client.

    BEFORE / SYNCHRONOUS FRAMEWORK
    // Simplified framework-style pseudocode
var home = Login();
var screen = home.OpenWindow("Settings");

Argue.AreEqual("Settings", () => screen.Title);
Argue.AreEqual(4, () => screen.VisibleTabCount);
Argue.IsTrue(() => screen.CodeField.IsRequired);

screen.CloseAndConfirm();
home.AssertBrowserWindowCount(1);
home.Logout();
    AFTER / INTENDED ASYNC FRAMEWORK
    // Illustrative; requires async retry overloads
var home = await LoginAsync();
var screen = await home.OpenWindowAsync<SettingsScreen>();

await Argue.AreEqual("Settings", () => screen.TitleAsync());
await Argue.AreEqual(4, () => screen.VisibleTabCountAsync());
await Argue.IsTrue(() => screen.CodeField.IsRequiredAsync());

await screen.CloseAsync();
await home.AssertBrowserTabCount();
await home.LogoutAsync();

    These excerpts explain a framework design; they are not standalone runnable tests or standard Playwright API examples. Internal paths, product-specific classes, and field identifiers have been omitted.

    Why the assertion shape matters.

    Awaiting a read is different from retrying an observation.

    // Reads once, then compares once
Assert.AreEqual(4, await ReadTabCountAsync());

// The helper can re-read while waiting
await Argue.AreEqual(4, () => ReadTabCountAsync());
    01

    Keep the observation inside the delegate

    A retry-capable helper invokes the delegate again on each attempt. Passing a previously read value cannot observe later UI changes.

    02

    Bound the wait and explain failure

    The custom helper needs a timeout, polling policy, async support, and useful diagnostics. Its name alone does not guarantee those behaviors.

    03

    Retry observations, not side effects

    Read titles, tab counts, and field state repeatedly. Keep login, navigation, save, and close actions outside assertion polling.

    Review migration parity explicitly.

    Source-level mapping and verification still required
    AreaMigration intentVerification required
    Session & navigationAsync login and typed window openingConfirm the same screen and authenticated state.
    Titles & tabsPreserve title, visibility, enabled-count, and selection checksConfirm async helpers re-observe the live UI.
    Fields & flagsPreserve focus, required, empty-value, and unchecked-state checksConfirm control adapters and default-state semantics.
    Close behaviorLegacy close/rebuild/confirmation becomes a different close operationEstablish behavioral equivalence; method names do not prove parity.
    CleanupUse await home.AssertBrowserTabCount(); after close, then log outVerify the helper's expected tab count, retry behavior, and diagnostics; use teardown for cleanup after assertion failures.
    Added coverageThe async example adds a tab-heading assertionRecord it as an addition rather than an unchanged assertion.

    What the evidence establishes.

    Supported: the source comparison illustrates a migration structure that preserves recognizable test intent and introduces async observation delegates.

    Unverified: compilation, deployed-client behavior, retry implementation, and cleanup parity. The supplied notes say the checked-in helper exposes synchronous signatures while the proposed version assumes async overloads.

    Next verification: confirm the helper contract, compile the test, run against the target client, exercise delayed rendering and a timeout failure, and validate teardown. A passing source review is not an executed test result.
